paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When you read do you also listen to music? Do you talk to friends or colleagues at the office? As you are reading online, are you also emailing or instant-messaging? Since the 1990s, virtually all of us have spent part of our day multitasking - that is, either switching from one task to another or juggling two or more things at the same time. Although doing many things at once can be a way of making tasks fun and energizing, according to author Thomas Lehman, You sacrifice focus when you do this. Multitasking is shifting focus from one task to another in rapid succession. It gives the illusion that you’re simultaneously tasking, but you’re not really. You can only shift back and forth. It’s like playing tennis with three balls.’ Of course, it depends on what you’re doing. For some people, listening to music while working actually makes them more imaginative because they are using their brains for different cognitive functions. But we’re all familiar with what Lehman calls ‘email voice’, when someone you’re talking to on the phone suddenly appears not to be fully engaged with the conversation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: We all know that computers and their spin-offs, the smartphone and cellphone, have created a very different world from several decades ago, when a desk worker had a typewriter, a phone and an occasional colleague who dropped into the office. Think even of the home in the days before the cordless phone. Those old enough can remember when talking on the land line meant sitting down, putting your feet up and chatting – not doing laundry, cooking dinner, sweeping the floor or answering the door as well.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: But today, as we feel required to do more and more things in a shorter period of time, researchers are trying to figure out how the brain changes attention from one subject to another. Earl Miller, professor of neuroscience at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, explains that humans have a very large prefrontal cortex, which is the part of the brain that helps us switch and prioritize tasks. In humans, he says, this area is about one-third of the entire cortex, while in dogs and cats, it is four or five percent and in monkeys about 15 percent. ‘With the growth of the prefrontal cortex, animals become more flexible in their behavior,’ according to Miller. We can do a couple of things at the same time if they are routine, but once they demand more cognitive processing, even the human brain has ‘a severe bottleneck’. Miller conducted studies where electrodes were attached to the heads of people to monitor them while performing different tasks. He found that when there’re lots of visual stimulants out there in front of you, only one or two objects tend to activate your neurons, indicating that you’re really only focusing on one or two items at a time.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: David Meyer, professor of psychology at the University of Michigan, looked at young adults as they performed tasks that involved doing math or classifying geometrical objects. The study found that for all task types, the participants lost time when they had to move from one undertaking to another, and that it took significantly longer to complete what they were doing when switching between more complicated tasks. If we’re talking about doing two jobs requiring real concentration, like text-messaging and driving, this lost time, even a fraction of a second, can be fatal. The RAC, a British non-profit organization that focuses on driving issues, asked drivers to use a driving simulator to see how texting affected their driving. In fact, the participants’ reaction time was increased by 35 percent when writing a text message.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Although we may be advised to focus on one thing at a time, the real world doesn’t work that way. We are constantly interrupted. Gloria Mark, professor of informatics at the University of California, has studied this using people in offices as subjects. Mark found that the people were interrupted and moved from one project or task to another about every 11 minutes. According to Mark, ‘People actually performed faster in conditions where they were interrupted, but they were less efficient.’ Mark also found that people were as likely to self-interrupt as to be interrupted by someone else. As the researchers watched, every 12 minutes or so, for no apparent reason, a person working on a document would turn and call someone or write an email. After only 20 minutes of uninterrupted work, people reported significantly higher stress, frustration and pressure. Mark says that further research needs to be done to explain these work patterns, but points out that ‘our increasingly shorter attention spans probably have something to do with it.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Psychiatrist Edward Hallowell has termed the effects of multitasking ‘attention deficit trait’, which he attributes entirely to the environment. ‘Our minds fill with noise - brain activity with little significance - and the brain gradually loses its capacity to attend fully to anything.’ Desperately trying to keep up with a multitude of jobs, we ‘feel a constant low level of panic and guilt.’ But Hallowell says that despite our belief that we cannot control this overload, we can. ‘We need to create boundaries,’ he says. That means devices like cellphones being banned at meetings. It means training yourself not to look at your computer every 20 seconds.
